The statement is **true**.

**Proof.**

Recall the relevant definitions. For a linear map $T: V \to W$, the **dual map** (transpose) is $T^*: W^* \to V^*$ defined by
$$T^*(\varphi) = \varphi \circ T, \qquad \varphi \in W^*.$$
The **annihilator** of a subspace $U \subseteq V$ is
$$U^0 = \{\, \psi \in V^* : \psi(u) = 0 \text{ for all } u \in U \,\}.$$

We must show $\operatorname{Im}(T^*) \subseteq (\ker T)^0$.

Let $\psi \in \operatorname{Im}(T^*)$. By definition of the image, there exists $\varphi \in W^*$ such that $\psi = T^*(\varphi) = \varphi \circ T$. To prove $\psi \in (\ker T)^0$, we must show $\psi$ vanishes on every vector in $\ker T$.

Take any $v \in \ker T$. Then $T(v) = 0_W$, and so
$$\psi(v) = (\varphi \circ T)(v) = \varphi(T(v)) = \varphi(0_W) = 0,$$
since $\varphi$ is linear. Thus $\psi$ annihilates every element of $\ker T$, i.e. $\psi \in (\ker T)^0$.

Since $\psi \in \operatorname{Im}(T^*)$ was arbitrary, we conclude
$$\operatorname{Im}(T^*) \subseteq (\ker T)^0.$$

**Remark.** The hypothesis that $V$ is finite-dimensional is not needed for this inclusion; it holds for arbitrary linear maps. (Finiteness of $\dim V$ is only relevant for the *reverse* inclusion $(\ker T)^0 \subseteq \operatorname{Im}(T^*)$, which together with the above gives the standard equality $\operatorname{Im}(T^*) = (\ker T)^0$ when $V$ is finite-dimensional.) Hence the stated inclusion is certainly true under the given hypothesis.
